explanation: **Leopold II** (king 1865-1909) ruled the Congo Free State from 1885 to 1908.

stem: Describe how Leopold II gained control of the Congo.

points.description: Set up the International African Association (1876), presented as scientific and humanitarian.
Hired Stanley (1879-1884) to build stations and obtain treaties from local rulers.
Promised free trade and presented himself as a humanitarian to the powers.
The Berlin Conference (1884-85) recognised his claim; the Congo Free State was set up in 1885 as his personal possession.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: In 1876 Leopold set up the International African Association, which he presented as a scientific and humanitarian body. He hired Stanley, who between 1879 and 1884 built stations along the Congo River and obtained treaties from hundreds of local rulers. Leopold promised the other powers free trade and presented himself as a humanitarian, and during the Berlin Conference of 1884-85 they recognised his claim. In 1885 the Congo Free State was established as his personal possession.

stem: Explain why the population of the Congo fell under Leopold's rule.

points.description: Identifies killings / violence by the Force Publique and company sentries.
Explains that villages failing quotas were punished and burned, and people killed.
Identifies famine / disease / falling births.
Explains that men forced to collect rubber could not farm, so food ran short, and people who fled were exposed to hunger and epidemics such as sleeping sickness.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Many people were killed by the Force Publique and company sentries enforcing rubber quotas, and villages that failed were burned. Even more died indirectly: men were forced into the forest for weeks to collect rubber, so they could not farm and food ran short, and people who fled their villages faced hunger. Weakened communities were hit by epidemics such as sleeping sickness, and births fell. Estimates of the total loss vary widely, but many historians judge it to have been millions.

hints: Violence was one cause; think about what happened to farming and health.

stem: Explain why Leopold II lost control of the Congo in 1908.

points.description: Identifies evidence from missionaries and visitors (Williams, Sheppard, Harris's photographs).
Explains that this evidence shocked the public in Britain and the USA.
Identifies the work of Morel, Casement and the Congo Reform Association.
Explains that the Casement Report (1904) gave official confirmation and mass meetings increased pressure on governments.
Identifies the 1905 commission of inquiry / pressure on Belgium.
Explains that Leopold's own commission confirmed abuses, so the Belgian parliament voted to annex the Congo.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Evidence of abuses came from missionaries and visitors: George Washington Williams wrote to Leopold in 1890, and missionaries such as Alice Seeley Harris sent home photographs of mutilated people that shocked the public. E. D. Morel worked out from shipping records that rubber was being taken by force, and the British consul Roger Casement's report of 1904 gave official confirmation. Morel and Casement founded the Congo Reform Association, which held mass meetings in Britain and the USA and pressed governments to act. Finally Leopold's own commission of inquiry confirmed many abuses in 1905, so the Belgian parliament, under international pressure, voted to annex the Congo in 1908.

stem:
Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a statement issued by a fictional press office in Brussels acting for the Congo Free State, 1904 (invented for this question)

> The Congo Free State has ended the Arab slave trade, built stations and steamers, and brought order where there was chaos. Isolated abuses by a few agents have been punished. The campaign against the State is the work of British merchants jealous of our success and of missionaries who wish to rule in our place.

**Source B** — a diary entry by a fictional Swedish engineer working on a Congo steamer, 1902, published after his death (invented for this question)

> At the post today the sentries brought in a line of women tied by the neck. The agent told me they will be released when their husbands bring the rubber that is owed. He receives a bonus for every kilo above the quota. He said this without shame, as one talks of the weather.

A's claims contradicted by the Casement Report (1904) and Leopold's own commission (1905).

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Source A was issued in 1904 on behalf of the Congo Free State, just as the Casement Report was published and the Congo Reform Association was founded, so its purpose was to defend Leopold's regime and discredit its critics. Its claim that abuses were isolated is contradicted by the Casement Report and by Leopold's own commission of inquiry, which confirmed many abuses in 1905. Source B is a private diary by an eyewitness, with no obvious reason to invent what he saw, although it was published after his death and may have been edited. What it describes, hostage-taking and bonuses for agents, matches what I know about the rubber system. It describes only one post, but Source B is clearly the more reliable.

parts.explanation: Reliability judged from provenance and from content checked against own knowledge.

hints: Ask who produced each source and why it was produced.

Villages given rubber quotas; men forced to collect wild rubber for little or no pay.
Enforced by the Force Publique and sentries: hostages, flogging (chicotte), burning villages, killings, severed hands.
Agents paid bonuses by results; huge profits for Leopold.

parts.stem: "The Congo Free State was the worst example of European rule in Africa." How far do you agree? Explain your answer.

points.description: Agree: scale of violence and population loss (estimates of millions).
Agree: private rule for profit with no outside control; whole system built on forced labour.
Disagree: forced labour, taxes and violence elsewhere (French indigénat; chibharo in Rhodesia; brutal wars of conquest).
Disagree: Belgian rule after 1908 remained exploitative; comparison is difficult because sources differ.
Supported judgement.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
There are strong reasons to agree. In the Congo Free State, forced labour was not a side effect but the basis of the whole economy. Rubber quotas were enforced by the Force Publique and company sentries through hostage-taking, flogging, the burning of villages and killings. The population fell severely; estimates vary, but many historians believe millions died from violence, famine and disease. Because the colony was Leopold's private property, there was no parliament or press at home to restrain him until the international campaign began.

However, the Congo was not unique. Forced labour existed in French territories under the indigénat and in Southern Rhodesia, where Africans called it chibharo. Wars of conquest elsewhere were extremely violent, and other colonies used taxes to push Africans into wage labour. Even after Belgium took over in 1908, the Congo remained an exploitative colony with no political rights for Africans. Comparing colonies is difficult because the evidence differs.

Overall I largely agree. Other colonial systems were harsh, but the Congo Free State combined private profit, an economy based entirely on forced extraction and very high loss of life in a way that made it an extreme case, which is why it provoked an international campaign.

parts.explanation: Both sides and a supported judgement for the top level.

hints: In (b), compare the Congo with French and British rule and ask what made it different.
